facts.fact_text: On 14 July 2008 a demonstration was held in Diyarbakır.
According to the police report of 21 July 2008, people started to assemble by 4.30 p.m. on 14 July 2008 in front of the DTP party office in Diyarbakır.
According to the police report of 21 July 2008, by 5.50 p.m. on 14 July 2008 approximately 3,000 people had gathered in front of the DTP party office in Diyarbakır.
According to the police report of 21 July 2008, demonstrators started to march and arrived at Koşuyolu Park at 6.30 p.m. on 14 July 2008, where the press statement was made.
In his statement of 22 July 2008, the applicant stated that he joined the demonstrators and chanted the slogan "Long live President Öcalan" ("Biji Serok Apo") on 14 July 2008.

During the hearing of 21 October 2008, the applicant maintained that he had participated in the demonstration, chanted the slogan "Long live President Öcalan" ("Biji Serok Apo") and thrown stones at the police when they intervened.
The applicant was arrested on 21 July 2008.

The judge of the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court remanded the applicant in custody on 22 July 2008 in view of the existence of a strong suspicion that he had committed the offence of "committing an offence on behalf of an illegal organisation without being a member of the organisation", in breach of Law no. 2911 (Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act).
On 22 July 2008 the Diyarbakır public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against the applicant with the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court.

The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court convicted the applicant under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), on the basis of Articles 220 § 6 and 314 § 3 of the same Code; section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713); and sections 23(b) and 33(c) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911).
The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court sentenced the applicant to a total of seven years and six months of imprisonment.
On 6 October 2009 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of 11 November 2008 of the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court.
Following the suspension of the execution of the applicant's sentence on 26 July 2010, the applicant was released from prison.

The applicant was charged with membership of an illegal organisation as he was considered to have committed a crime on behalf of an illegal organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) on the basis of Articles 220 § 6 and 314 § 3 of the same Code.
The applicant was charged with resisting the security forces by way of throwing stones under sections 23(b) and 33(c) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911).
The applicant was charged with disseminating propaganda in support of the PKK under section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713).

At the material time, Article 220 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who establishes or directs organisations for the purpose of criminal activity shall be liable to imprisonment of between two and six years, provided that the structure of the organisation, the number of members, and the quantity of equipment and supplies are sufficient to commit the intended crimes.

At the material time, Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who commits a crime on behalf of the illegal organisation, even if they are not a member of that organisation, shall also be punished for being a member of the organisation.

Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provides that anyone who becomes a member of an armed organisation mentioned in Article 314 § 1 shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between five and ten years.

According to section 23(b) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), in force at the material time, meetings or demonstration marches during which the demonstrators or the participants bear, inter alia, firearms, explosives, cutting and perforating tools, stones, bats, iron or rubber bars, wires, chains, poisons, gas or fog materials, were considered to be "unlawful meetings and demonstration marches".

Section 33(c) of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), before it was amended by Law no. 6008 on 25 July 2010, provided that persons who show resistance with weapons or materials listed in section 23(b) while being dispersed during meetings and demonstration marches shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between five and eight years.

At the material time, section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) provided that any person who disseminates propaganda in support of a terrorist organisation shall be liable to a term of imprisonment of between one and five years.

At the material time, according to Article 250 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Law no. 5271) and section 4 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713), assize courts with special jurisdiction were competent to try a number of crimes, including the crimes proscribed by Article 314 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) and section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713).
The PKK (Kurdish Workers' Party) is an illegal armed organisation.
The police took the necessary measures on 14 July 2008 as they suspected that there could be violent protests during the march, which could become a demonstration for the PKK.

According to the police report of 21 July 2008, at 7 p.m. on 14 July 2008, while Emine Ayna, a Member of Parliament from the DTP, was giving a speech, a group of people started throwing stones at the police officers and the cars parked in the neighbourhood.

According to the police report of 21 July 2008, subsequent to the press statements on 14 July 2008, when the crowd dispersed, some people within the crowd knocked over waste containers and attacked the police and the shops in the neighbourhood with stones and bats while chanting slogans in support of the PKK and its leader.

The judge of the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court remanded the applicant in custody on 22 July 2008 in view of the existence of a strong suspicion that he had committed the offence of "committing an offence on behalf of an illegal organisation without being a member of the organisation", in breach of Law no. 2911 (Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act).

The judge of the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court remanded the applicant in custody on 22 July 2008 in view of the existence of a strong suspicion that he had committed the offence of "dissemination of propaganda in support of a terrorist organisation", and having regard to the evidence.

The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court found in its judgment of 11 November 2008 that on 11 July 2008 the Fırat News Agency, controlled by the PKK, published a declaration of the Democratic People's Initiative of Turkey and Kurdistan containing instructions to hold marches on 14 July 2008 to show respect for Abdullah Öcalan, with the nature of Serhildan (rebellion).

The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court established in its judgment of 11 November 2008 that the applicant (Ferit Gülcü) actively took part in the illegal demonstrations held on 14 July 2008 in Diyarbakır in accordance with the instructions of the terrorist organisation PKK.
The applicant was born in 1992.
The applicant was transferred to the children's branch of the Security Directorate after being found to be a minor subsequent to a medical check following his arrest on 21 July 2008.
In his statement of 22 July 2008, the applicant stated that he joined the demonstrators and chanted the slogan "Long live President Öcalan" ("Biji Serok Apo") on 14 July 2008.
In his statement of 22 July 2008, the applicant stated that he threw stones at the police officers on 14 July 2008.

In his statement of 22 July 2008, the applicant stated that he did not have any particular purpose when he chanted the slogan and threw stones at the police, and that he only acted together with the crowd.
In his statement of 22 July 2008, the applicant stated that he did not know why there was a demonstration and that he had no connection with any illegal organisation.

The applicant was charged with membership of an illegal organisation as he was considered to have committed a crime on behalf of an illegal organisation under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) on the basis of Articles 220 § 6 and 314 § 3 of the same Code.

During the hearing of 21 October 2008, the applicant maintained that he had participated in the demonstration, chanted the slogan "Long live President Öcalan" ("Biji Serok Apo") and thrown stones at the police when they intervened.
The public prosecutor requested that the sentences be reduced taking into account the fact that the applicant had been aged between 15 and 18 years old at the material time.

The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court established in its judgment of 11 November 2008 that the applicant (Ferit Gülcü) actively took part in the illegal demonstrations held on 14 July 2008 in Diyarbakır in accordance with the instructions of the terrorist organisation PKK.

The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court established in its judgment of 11 November 2008 that the applicant chanted the slogan "Long live President Öcalan" ("Biji Serok Apo") together with the crowd on 14 July 2008.
The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court established in its judgment of 11 November 2008 that the applicant attacked the police with stones on 14 July 2008.

The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court concluded in its judgment of 11 November 2008 that the applicant's acts, committed within the knowledge and in line with the will of the PKK organisation, were perpetrated on behalf of the organisation, and that the applicant should be convicted under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) with reference to Articles 314 § 3 and 220 § 6 of the same Code.

The Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court convicted the applicant of membership of an illegal organisation pursuant to Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) on the basis of Articles 220 § 6 and 314 § 3 of the same Code, finding it established that the applicant had taken part in the events of 14 July 2008 which had become propaganda in support of the illegal organisation, upon the call made by the PKK.

For the membership of an illegal organisation conviction, the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court applied the minimum penalty of five years' imprisonment, then increased it by one and a half times by virtue of section 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) to seven years and six months.

For the membership of an illegal organisation conviction, the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court reduced the sentence by one third by virtue of Article 31 § 3 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), taking into account that the applicant had been aged between 15 and 18 at the material time, resulting in five years.

For the membership of an illegal organisation conviction, the Fifth Division of Diyarbakır Assize Court further reduced the sentence by one sixth under Article 62 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) taking into account the applicant's "sincere confessions" as well as his attitude and behaviour during the proceedings, resulting in a total of four years and two months of imprisonment.

At the material time, Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) provided that anyone who commits a crime on behalf of the illegal organisation, even if they are not a member of that organisation, shall also be punished for being a member of the organisation.

Diyarbakır Assize Court stated in its judgment of 31 May 2007 in the case of F.Ö. that in cases where people participate in funerals of members of a terrorist organisation or in Newroz celebrations subsequent to abstract and generalised calls of that organisation, and where chanting slogans constitutes propaganda for that organisation, it is not possible to state that those crimes were committed on behalf of the organisation.

Diyarbakır Assize Court stated in its judgment of 31 May 2007 in the case of F.Ö. that in order for a court to conclude that a crime was committed on behalf of an organisation, the organisation must have called for action not to an undefined collective, but rather to an individual person who is capable of directly committing that act.

The Plenary Court of Cassation (Criminal Divisions) held in its decision of 4 March 2008 that the PKK's public call had been made concrete through broadcasts from media organs of the organisation and there is no need for such calls to target identified individual persons.

The Plenary Court of Cassation (Criminal Divisions) held in its decision of 4 March 2008 that the acts carried out on behalf of the PKK were within the knowledge of the organisation and in line with its will, and that the acts of an accused who participates in such acts constitute a breach of Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) on the basis of Articles 220 § 6 and 314 § 3 of the same Code.

Article 3 § 1 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child provides that in all actions concerning children, whether undertaken by public or private social welfare institutions, courts of law, administrative authorities or legislative bodies, the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration.

Article 37(b) of the Convention on the Rights of the Child provides that no child shall be deprived of his or her liberty unlawfully or arbitrarily, and that the arrest, detention or imprisonment of a child shall be in conformity with the law and shall be used only as a measure of last resort and for the shortest appropriate period of time.

Article 40 § 1 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child provides that States Parties recognize the right of every child alleged as, accused of, or recognized as having infringed the penal law to be treated in a manner consistent with the promotion of the child's sense of dignity and worth, which reinforces the child's respect for the human rights and fundamental freedoms of others and which takes into account the child's age and the desirability of promoting the child's reintegration and the child's assuming a constructive role in society.

Article 40 § 4 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child provides that a variety of dispositions, such as care, guidance and supervision orders, counselling, probation, foster care, education and vocational training programmes and other alternatives to institutional care shall be available to ensure that children are dealt with in a manner appropriate to their well-being and proportionate both to their circumstances and the offence.

General Comment No. 10 of the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child, dated 25 April 2007, states that children in conflict with the law have the right to be treated in ways that promote their reintegration and the child's assuming a constructive role in society, and that the arrest, detention or imprisonment of a child may be used only as a measure of last resort.

General Comment No. 10 of the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child, dated 25 April 2007, states that when judicial proceedings are initiated, the juvenile justice system should provide for ample opportunities to deal with children in conflict with the law by using social and/or educational measures, and to strictly limit the use of deprivation of liberty, and in particular pre-trial detention, as a measure of last resort.

General Comment No. 10 of the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child, dated 25 April 2007, states that the reaction to an offence should always be in proportion not only to the circumstances and the gravity of the offence, but also to the age, lesser culpability, circumstances and needs of the child, as well as to the various and particularly long-term needs of the society, and that a strictly punitive approach is not in accordance with the leading principles for juvenile justice.

In his report published on 1 October 2009 (CommDH(2009)30), following his visit to Turkey on 28 June to 3 July 2009, Mr Thomas Hammarberg, the former Commissioner for Human Rights of the Council of Europe, stated that over the previous nine months approximately 250 children of Kurdish origin, more than 190 of them between 13 and 17 years of age, had been arrested and detained after having taken part in demonstrations organised by Kurdish groups and thrown stones at police forces.

In his report published on 1 October 2009 (CommDH(2009)30), Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that four children aged between 16 and 17 had been detained in the Diyarbakır prison since 14 July 2008, charged with membership of a terrorist organization as a result of participating in a protest in Diyarbakır.

In his report published on 1 October 2009 (CommDH(2009)30), Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that prosecution in such cases is often based on Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), and that the extensive use of this provision by courts against participants of Kurdish-related demonstrations follows a ruling of the General Criminal Board of the Court of Cassation in March 2008.

In his report published on 10 January 2012 (CommDH(2012)2), Mr Thomas Hammarberg stated that persons participating in demonstrations following public calls by the PKK were brought into the ambit of Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), in accordance with a ruling of the Court of Cassation in March 2008.

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that many hundreds of people in Turkey face prosecution or are serving substantial sentences for terrorism convictions for engaging in peaceful protest or throwing stones or burning a tire at a protest, and that legal amendments since 2005 and case law since 2008 have allowed courts to convict demonstrators under the harshest terrorism laws.

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that criminal justice officials have deemed Kurdish protestors to be 'committing crimes on behalf of the PKK without being a member of that organization' under Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237), resulting in prosecution as if they were armed 'members' of the PKK under Article 314 § 2 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237).

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that the majority of adults convicted under these laws have received prison terms of between seven and 15 years, and that prior to a July 2010 legal amendment, child protestors typically received prison sentences of between four and five years.

The Human Rights Watch report of 1 November 2010 stated that in none of the cases examined by Human Rights Watch had prosecutors submitted evidence to establish that the individual defendant either heard the PKK's 'appeal' or had been directly instructed or motivated by the PKK to participate in the demonstration, or had any other specific link with the PKK.

The Amnesty International report of 17 June 2010 stated that children alleged to have participated in demonstrations are frequently prosecuted under section 7(2) of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713) and under Article 314 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) via Article 220 § 6 of the same Code, following a ruling of the Supreme Court of Appeals (case number 2007/9282).

The Amnesty International report of 17 June 2010 stated that children who have been prosecuted in connection with their participation in demonstrations have frequently faced multiple charges for the same act, including making propaganda for a terrorist organisation, membership of a terrorist organisation and violation of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911).

The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) allows the state to punish individuals who have not been proven in court to be members of a terrorist organisation as though they were, if deemed to have performed a criminal act 'in the name of an organization'.

The Amnesty International report of 27 March 2013 stated that courts have used Article 220 § 6 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) as the basis for imposing increased sentences with little evidence of the commission of a recognizably criminal offence or any demonstrable link to a 'terrorist organization', and that the evidence frequently amounts to nothing more than participation in demonstrations or the writing of pro-Kurdish articles.
